content: Hepatitis D is a disease caused by a small circular RNA virus known as the hepatitis delta virus (HDV). This virus is unique in that it is considered a subviral satellite, as it requires the presence of the hepatitis B virus (HBV) to propagate. HDV can be transmitted either through simultaneous infection with HBV (coinfection) or by infecting an individual already chronically infected with HBV (superinfection). Both coinfection and superinfection with HDV result in more severe complications compared to HBV infection alone. These complications include an increased risk of acute liver failure and a higher likelihood of developing liver cancer in chronic infections. When combined with HBV, hepatitis D has the highest mortality rate among all hepatitis infections, reaching up to 20%. The hepatitis D virus was first identified in 1977 by an Italian researcher, Mario Rizzetto. Despite limited understanding of its pathogenesis, it is believed that both the adaptive and innate immune systems play a critical role in the liver damage caused by HDV. The virus exclusively targets the liver, as it is the only organ where HDV can replicate. HBV is an essential cofactor in the progression of liver damage, and dual infection with HBV and HDV leads to more severe liver injury than HBV infection alone. Certain genotypes of HDV may exhibit cytopathic effects. HDV is transmitted through percutaneous exposure, sexual contact, or contact with infected blood or blood products. Rarely, perinatal transmission may occur. The infectivity of HDV is influenced by its genotype, which affects viral assembly. The hepatitis D virus belongs to the genus Deltavirus and has a single-stranded circular RNA genome with a high degree of complementarity, allowing it to survive at high temperatures. Its life cycle depends on cooperation with the host cell at all stages, including attachment, penetration, uncoating, replication, assembly, and release of new virions. HDV replication also requires the presence of a hepadnavirus, such as HBV, to provide the protein components for its envelope. The virus is composed of several particles, including HBsAg, HDAg-S, HDAg-L, and RNA. Different HDV genotypes are associated with varying disease courses. The virus has a specific tropism for hepatocytes, and humans are its natural reservoir. Hepatitis D must be differentiated from other diseases that cause similar symptoms, such as fever, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, elevated liver enzymes (ALT and AST), and icteric sclera. These conditions include other viral hepatitis infections, alcoholic hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis. HDV infection affects over 15 million people worldwide who are chronically infected with HBV. Regions with high rates of HDV infection include Central Africa, the Mediterranean Basin, the Amazon Basin, and parts of Asia. The prevalence of HDV is decreasing in many areas due to HBV vaccination programs, improved education and awareness, and better socioeconomic conditions. Risk factors for HDV infection include intravenous drug use, infection during pregnancy, sexual contact with infected individuals, exposure to unscreened blood or blood products, hemodialysis, and occupational exposure among healthcare and public service workers. Screening is not necessary for the general population with low risk of HBV and HDV infection. However, individuals who are HBsAg-positive with acute or chronic hepatitis, or those who are HBsAg-negative but IgM anti-HBc-positive, should be screened for HDV. Blood products should also be screened to prevent transmission through transfusions or hemodialysis. HDV is a defective virus that requires prior or concurrent HBV infection. Its clinical manifestations are similar to those of HBV, including fatigue, lethargy, nausea, jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine. The disease progresses through four phases: incubation, preicteric, icteric, and convalescence. Coinfection with HBV and HDV can result in acute hepatitis B and D, with 95% of patients clearing the infection. Superinfection of an HBV carrier often leads to fulminant hepatitis, chronic active hepatitis, and progression to cirrhosis. Complications of HDV include chronic active hepatitis, fulminant hepatitis, hepatic cirrhosis, and liver failure. The mortality rate for HDV infection is higher than that of HBV, ranging from 2% to 20%. Hepatitis D can only occur in patients who are simultaneously or previously infected with HBV. Common symptoms include fever, yellowing of the eyes and skin, fatigue, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, and dark urine. Coinfection is associated with a more severe disease course, often leading to fulminant hepatitis. In superinfection, symptoms may initially be nonspecific, and most cases progress to chronicity. Physical examination findings in acute HDV infection may be normal or include jaundice and joint impairment due to arthralgia. In chronic disease, findings depend on the stage and may include jaundice, palmar erythema, spider angiomas, gynecomastia, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites, peripheral edema, and asterixis. The diagnosis of hepatitis D is confirmed by detecting HDV RNA in circulation using RT-PCR. HBsAg levels can be monitored during treatment to evaluate response and determine therapy duration. After recovery, markers of HDV infection, such as IgM and IgG antibodies, disappear within months. Liver biopsy is indicated in HDV RNA-positive patients to assess the stage of liver disease, with findings similar to those in HBV infection. Coinfection with HIV and HCV should be ruled out in HDV-infected patients. Serologic markers, such as HDV RNA, HDAg, and IgM and IgG anti-HDV antibodies, may persist in chronic hepatitis D. Imaging studies, such as CT scans, MRI, and ultrasound, can be used to diagnose and monitor complications of HDV infection, including biliary obstruction, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. MRI findings may include a nodular liver appearance and signs of portal hypertension, such as ascites and splenomegaly. Ultrasound may reveal hepatomegaly, gallbladder wall thickening, increased echogenicity, and signs of portal hypertension. HBsAg carriers with cirrhosis should undergo echographic evaluation every six months. Identifying the genotype of HDV helps predict disease severity and response to treatment. Endoscopy may be useful in advanced disease stages to evaluate for esophageal varices in patients with liver cirrhosis. Currently, there is no effective antiviral therapy for acute or chronic hepatitis D. Interferon-α is the only drug with antiviral activity against HDV, but most patients remain HDV RNA-positive despite health improvements. Long-term treatment with nucleos(t)ide analogs (NUCs) has shown a decline in HBsAg levels in some patients. Chronic hepatitis D patients should be treated with weekly injections of pegylated interferon for at least 48 weeks. Surgical treatment is not part of hepatitis D management. However, certain procedures, such as peritoneal drainage, may be indicated for complications like ascites. Liver transplantation may be necessary for end-stage liver disease, liver failure secondary to HDV infection, or hepatocellular carcinoma in patients for whom interferon treatment is not indicated. Prevention of HDV infection relies on HBV vaccination, as HDV requires HBV for infection. Individuals infected with HBV should avoid risk behaviors, such as contact with infected blood and sharing sharp objects, to prevent superinfection. Considering the progression of symptomatic hepatitis D to cirrhosis, liver failure, and hepatocellular carcinoma, research into effective therapeutic regimens and new drugs with better efficacy, fewer side effects, and lower costs is essential and cost-effective. Future therapies for HDV may target post-translational modification and viral assembly. New drugs, such as prenylation inhibitors, HBV entry inhibitors, and novel forms of interferons, are under investigation for improved efficacy and tolerability in treating hepatitis D.
